subject: biology

assetStrategy.specDefaultBucket: GLB/GLTF (spec §21 assigns 'cell' models to this bucket)
assetStrategy.deviationRationale: The red blood cell's biconcave disc is a clean lathe/revolve primitive built from a parametric profile curve (see assetBrief), not an organic sculpt — closer in kind to the 'molecule/planet-tier' primitives the spec reserves procedural Three.js for than to the sculpted anatomy GLBs it reserves the GLB/GLTF bucket for.
assetStrategy.integrationNote: Because there is no static mesh export, 'url' below is null and the generation approach lives entirely in assetBrief as buildable geometry/material instructions, not export guidance. If this is reversed to match the spec default and sibling cell-biology components (e.g. neuron's neuron.glb), 'url' becomes a standard '/assets/models/biology/cell-biology/red-blood-cell/red-blood-cell.glb' path and assetBrief should be rewritten as sculpting/export guidance instead of procedural-geometry code guidance.

layers: Cytoplasm / Hemoglobin Fill (interior volume, revealed through translucency and on cross-section)
Cross-Section Cutaway (half-cell showing the biconcave profile and confirming the absence of a nucleus)

hotspots.label: Cell Membrane
hotspots.description: The thin, flexible outer boundary of the cell, sitting at the rim where the disc is thickest and visible as the outer silhouette edge from any camera angle.
hotspots.function: A phospholipid bilayer studded with proteins that lets the cell bend and squeeze through capillaries narrower than its own resting diameter without breaking.
hotspots.positionHint: On the outer rim of the disc at the equator (the widest point, roughly the 3 o'clock position relative to the default camera), sitting directly on the surface silhouette so the dot reads against the off-white background.

hotspots.label: Hemoglobin
hotspots.description: Fills the interior of the cell, most visible through the shallow, more translucent dimple on the front face, and fully revealed in cross-section as the solid crimson core.
hotspots.function: An iron-rich protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in body tissues — the cell's entire functional purpose and the source of blood's red color.
hotspots.positionHint: Centered on the front face, in the shallow dimple where the membrane is thinnest and most translucent, so the deeper crimson interior tone reads through the surface even before cross-section is engaged.

hotspots.label: Biconcave Shape
hotspots.description: The defining silhouette of the whole cell, most visible at the thin, pinched edge of the disc where the top and bottom dimples curve in toward the rim.
hotspots.function: Maximizes surface area relative to volume for faster gas exchange and lets the cell flex through vessels narrower than its resting width.
hotspots.positionHint: On the thin edge of the disc, at the point of tightest curvature where the top and bottom concave faces pinch in toward the rim — best seen from a slightly rotated three-quarter angle, roughly the 5 o'clock edge position.

hotspots.label: Cytoplasm
hotspots.description: The fluid layer just inside the membrane, on the upper surface opposite the Hemoglobin hotspot so the two dots never collide; distinguishable mainly in cross-section as a thin band before the denser hemoglobin core.
hotspots.function: Provides the fluid medium in which hemoglobin is suspended; in a mature red blood cell it occupies nearly the entire interior since the nucleus and major organelles have been expelled.
hotspots.positionHint: On the upper surface near the center, opposite the Hemoglobin hotspot so the two dots don't visually collide, marking the fluid interior as distinct from the hemoglobin molecules suspended within it.

visualStyleNotes: Matches Anatomy Atelier's chrome and restraint level: warm off-white/cream backdrop (#F7F1E8-ish), the cell rendered large and centered (roughly 55-65% of viewport height), soft single-source studio lighting with gentle ambient fill and a faint soft-contact shadow beneath the cell — no rim glow, no bloom, no gradient halos. Material is matte-satin, not glossy plastic: subsurface-scattering-like translucency on the membrane (so hemoglobin color reads faintly through the dimples) but no specular hotspots or shininess (see materialNotes). Hotspot dots follow the reference's actual treatment, not a flattened simplification: a solid center dot with a soft radial glow halo, color-coded per hotspot rather than a single flat accent — Cell Membrane muted navy-blue (#5b7fb5), Hemoglobin muted orange (#d98a3d), Biconcave Shape muted purple (#8a6fa8), Cytoplasm muted leaf-green (#5f9e78), matching the reference's curated multi-hue dot family; dots sit flush on the surface and pulse very subtly if idle. Auto-rotate is slow and continuous (~1 full turn per 18-20s) with a toggle control matching the reference's bottom-right pill switch. Left-side tool rail (Rotate / Zoom / Isolate / Cross-section / Layers / Compare / Reset — 7 items, matching the reference's rail exactly and giving the White Blood Cell compare pairing a real entry point) and right-side info card follow the reference layout 1:1. Absolutely avoid: cartoon/gamey red blood cell tropes (googly eyes, cel-shading, thick black outlines), neon or saturated "traffic-cone" red, glossy toy-plastic shading, particle/glow effects for hemoglobin itself, or a cluttered scene with multiple cells — this is a single specimen study, not a bloodstream diorama.
materialNotes: Membrane: physically-based material, base color a warm dusty rose (#D89090 - #C97C7C range), moderate roughness (~0.45, matte-satin, not glossy), opacity ~0.55-0.65 with a simple fake-SSS trick (fresnel-driven opacity falloff so the rim reads more solid/saturated and the flat dimple faces read more translucent, letting interior hemoglobin color bleed through). No clearcoat, no strong specular. Hemoglobin / interior fill: a deeper saturated crimson (#A83232 - #8E2A2A range), fully opaque, subtle grain/noise micro-texture at low amplitude to suggest molecular density without reading as "particles" or glitter. Cytoplasm (only distinguishable in cross-section, as the thin fluid layer immediately inside the membrane before the denser hemoglobin core): a slightly lighter, warmer red-orange (#C05A4A range) at very low contrast against the hemoglobin fill — this is a subtle distinction, not a hard boundary. Background: warm off-white/cream (#F7F1E8), matching Anatomy Atelier's canvas exactly. Soft floor shadow beneath the cell, no cast shadow on a visible ground plane. Lighting: single soft key light from upper-front-left (~45°), low-intensity ambient/fill from the opposite side, no colored lighting, no rim light.
assetBrief:
ASSET STRATEGY NOTE: This is a flagged deviation from spec §21's default asset-strategy bucket (which assigns 'cell' models to GLB/GLTF) — see the top-level 'assetStrategy' field for the rationale and the integration note for what changes if this is reversed to a GLB pipeline. Confirm before build.

GEOMETRY & CONSTRUCTION (procedural, no sculpted mesh needed):
Build the cell as a lathe/revolve geometry from a 2D profile curve, not from primitive spheres/torii directly. Define the profile in the XY half-plane (X = radial distance from center axis, Y = height) using a biconcave-disc formula (the standard "Evans & Fung" / Cao parametric form works well):
  y(x) = ± 0.5 * sqrt(1 - (x/R)^2) * (C0 + C1*(x/R)^2 + C2*(x/R)^4)
with R ≈ 1.0 (normalized radius, then scaled to fill ~55% of viewport height at default camera distance), and C0/C1/C2 tuned so the profile shows: overall disc diameter noticeably greater than its thickness (roughly 3.5-4:1 diameter-to-max-thickness ratio), a pinched waist at the rim (edge thickness thinner than the torus-like rim bulge just inside it), and a visible central dimple on both faces (dimple depth roughly 15-20% of the rim bulge thickness — visible but not a deep hole). Revolve this profile 360° around the Y axis with 48-64 radial segments and 32+ profile segments for a smooth, non-faceted surface (this is a "molecule/planet-tier" primitive-built object per the procedural-three criteria, not an organic sculpt — no need for anatomical mesh sculpting or a glb pipeline).

Cross-section: implement via a clip-plane/stencil approach (a plane through the Y axis, e.g. clipping at Z=0) that reveals: (1) the hollow interior filled with a uniform hemoglobin-red volume (no nucleus, no organelles — this absence is itself the teaching point vs. other specialized cells), and (2) the true biconcave profile silhouette in cross-section, which is the clearest possible view of "Biconcave Shape."

PROPORTIONS: Keep the cell recognizably disc-shaped from the front (a slightly-shaded circle, not obviously biconcave from straight-on) and let the biconcave dimple and thin rim only become obvious on rotation or in cross-section — this mirrors how real RBC micrographs read and gives the auto-rotate a genuine "aha" moment rather than showing everything at once from the default angle.

REFERENCE MATCH: Follow assets/reference/anatomy-atelier/desktop-overview.png and desktop-interaction.png for chrome layout (left tool rail, right info card, bottom auto-rotate pill, serif "specimen" wordmark styling) and for the exact restraint level of the 3D object itself — calm, single-material, no glow, no gradient mesh, no gamified color-coding of substructures beyond the four hotspot dots (see visualStyleNotes for the dot treatment, which does use a curated multi-hue palette with soft glow, matching the reference — not a single flat accent as an earlier draft of this brief incorrectly specified).

WHAT NOT TO DO: no nucleus (biologically incorrect — mature RBCs are anucleate, and this is a teaching point, not an oversight); no glossy toy-plastic or rubber-ball shading; no neon/saturated red; no visible polygon faceting (keep segment counts high enough for a smooth revolve); no multiple cells or bloodstream scene-setting; no glow/bloom/particle FX on hemoglobin; no cartoon eyes or anthropomorphizing; no busy internal organelle detail (a red blood cell's defining feature is precisely how empty/simple its interior is compared to other specialized cells in this unit).
